nodes.title: Drug Dosing in Renal Impairment
nodes.summary: This section provides non-clinical recommendations for adjusting drug dosages in renal impairment across various drug classes, including antimicrobials, cardiovascular agents, and analgesics. It also advises on assessing renal function and monitoring kidney status after dose changes.

children.title: Drug Dosing in Renal Impairment — Overview
children.summary: This synthetic test document provides plausible recommendations regarding drug dosing in renal impairment but explicitly states these are not clinical guidance and must never be used for patient care.
children.content:
> **SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT — NOT CLINICAL GUIDANCE.** Written to exercise the
> ingest, indexing and retrieval pipeline. The recommendations below are
> plausible in shape but must never be used for patient care.

children.title: Assessing Renal Function
children.summary: This section advises which formula to use for drug dosing in renal impairment, recommending Cockcroft–Gault over eGFR. It also discusses limitations of serum creatinine, such as its lag time and inaccuracy in certain patient populations.

children.title: Which Estimate to Use
children.summary: The passage advises using the Cockcroft–Gault estimate for drug dosing in renal impairment instead of the laboratory's eGFR because eGFR normalizes to 1.73 m² and inaccurately estimates clearance for different body sizes.
children.content:
Use the Cockcroft–Gault estimate of creatinine clearance for drug dosing, not the
eGFR reported automatically by the laboratory. Reported eGFR is normalised to a
body surface area of 1.73 m² and misleads at the extremes of body size — it
overestimates clearance in a small elderly woman and underestimates it in a large
young man.

children.title: When Creatinine Misleads
children.summary: The passage discusses limitations of serum creatinine for assessing renal function, noting its 24-48 hour lag in acute kidney injury and underestimation in patients with low muscle mass like the elderly or malnourished.
children.content:
Serum creatinine lags behind a falling glomerular filtration rate by 24–48 hours.
In acute kidney injury, dose on the trajectory rather than the current value: a
creatinine that has doubled in a day represents a far lower clearance than the
absolute number suggests.

Creatinine also underestimates impairment in patients with low muscle mass —
the elderly, the malnourished, amputees, and those with cirrhosis.

children.title: Antimicrobials
children.summary: This section covers antimicrobial dosing adjustments in renal impairment for various drug classes. It provides specific guidelines for aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, and vancomycin regarding interval changes, dose reduction, and target trough levels based on kidney function.

children.title: Aminoglycosides
children.summary: This passage details gentamicin dosing in renal impairment, recommending an extended interval rather than dose reduction. It specifies taking a trough level before the second dose if clearance is below 30 mL/min and monitoring for vestibular toxicity daily.
children.content:
Gentamicin is dosed at 5–7 mg/kg using ideal body weight, with the interval
extended rather than the dose reduced. Extending the interval preserves the peak
concentration that drives bacterial killing while allowing a trough low enough to
limit accumulation.

Take a trough level before the second dose where clearance is below 30 mL/min.
Stop if the trough exceeds 1 mg/L, and do not simply give the next dose on time.

Monitor for vestibular toxicity daily. It is frequently irreversible and is
detected late if the only monitoring is biochemical.

children.title: Beta-Lactams
children.summary: The passage advises dose reduction for penicillins and cephalosporins when renal clearance is below 30 mL/min, recommending frequency adjustment over dose reduction. It also notes that neurotoxicity symptoms like myoclonus can indicate beta-lactam accumulation.
children.content:
Most penicillins and cephalosporins require dose reduction below a clearance of
30 mL/min. Reduce the frequency rather than the individual dose, since efficacy
depends on the time the concentration stays above the minimum inhibitory
concentration.

Neurotoxicity — myoclonus, confusion, seizures — is the characteristic sign of
beta-lactam accumulation and is regularly misattributed to sepsis or delirium in
an unwell patient.

children.title: Vancomycin
children.summary: This passage details vancomycin dosing guidelines in renal impairment, recommending dose by area under the curve or a trough target of 15–20 mg/L for deep-seated infections, and advises post-dialysis dosing.
children.content:
Dose by area under the curve rather than by trough where the service supports it.
Where troughs are used, target 15–20 mg/L for deep-seated infection.

In dialysis, dose after the session, not before, or a substantial fraction of the
dose is removed by the filter.

children.title: Cardiovascular Agents
children.summary: The passage discusses dosing adjustments for cardiovascular agents in renal impairment, noting that atenolol and sotalol accumulate while bisoprolol and metoprolol are safer. It also covers digoxin's dose adjustment with potassium levels and expected creatinine rises with ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
children.content:
Renally cleared beta-blockers such as atenolol and sotalol accumulate; bisoprolol
and metoprolol are hepatically cleared and are safer choices in impairment.

Digoxin requires both a lower loading and a lower maintenance dose. Its toxic
threshold falls further with hypokalaemia, so the dose cannot be considered in
isolation from the potassium.

ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers reduce glomerular filtration
pressure by design. A creatinine rise of up to 30% after initiation is expected
and is not a reason to stop; a rise beyond that warrants review for renal artery
stenosis or volume depletion.

children.title: Analgesia
children.summary: The passage advises avoiding NSAIDs below 30 mL/min clearance due to kidney injury risk. It discusses morphine accumulation and recommends oxycodone or fentanyl over gabapentin and pregabalin for dosing adjustments in renal impairment.
children.content:
Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs entirely below a clearance of 30
mL/min. They are the single most common avoidable cause of drug-induced acute
kidney injury in inpatients.

Morphine accumulates as the active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide, causing
delayed sedation and respiratory depression up to 24 hours after the last dose.
Oxycodone and fentanyl are preferred. Gabapentin and pregabalin need substantial
reduction and are a frequent cause of unexplained drowsiness on the ward.

children.title: Monitoring After a Dose Change
children.summary: The passage advises rechecking renal function within 48 hours after dose adjustments or exposure to nephrotoxins, contrast, or hypotension. It also instructs documenting the clearance value and calculation date on the prescription.
children.content:
Recheck renal function within 48 hours of any dose adjustment, and again after
any new nephrotoxin, contrast exposure or episode of hypotension.

Document the clearance used and the date it was calculated on the prescription
itself, so that the next prescriber can see what the dose was based on rather
than recalculating from a stale value.
